speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: One of Singapore’s strengths lies in our being a vibrant international business and commercial hub that is open and connected to the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We must continue to be so, to ensure that our economy remains vibrant and growing, amidst global uncertainties and disruptions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Against this backdrop, one key area of focus in my Ministry's work has been to strengthen Singapore's legal and dispute resolution framework, to better serve the needs of international businesses that use Singapore as a base for their international commercial transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singapore is one of the leading cross-border dispute resolution centres in the world and undergirding this is our trusted legal system and the strong rule of law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We also provide a comprehensive suite of international dispute resolution services to meet the varying needs of businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As part of efforts to strengthen our dispute resolution ecosystem, Singapore has invested in the development of international commercial mediation, including through building up institutions, developing capabilities and also updating our laws.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the same vein, the Singapore Convention Signing Ceremony and Conference held in August last year was an important milestone for Singapore’s efforts in developing the dispute resolution landscape on at least two levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, on a broader level, the Convention demonstrated Singapore’s thought leadership in international rule of law efforts and helped raise our position as an international dispute resolution hub to a new level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In February 2018, the UN Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) Working Group on Dispute Settlement finalised the text of the Convention and the corresponding Model Law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singapore contributed significantly to the development of the Convention at UNCITRAL.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Working Group was chaired by a Singaporean, and the Singapore delegation participated actively in the negotiations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Local industry experts were involved in shaping Singapore’s positions on the Convention and also played an active role in contributing to the final outcome.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It took only three years between 2015 and 2018 to conclude an instrument dealing with enforcement of international settlement agreements resulting from mediation, when several past attempts failed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This exhibited the Working Group’s dedication to constructive and open dialogue in the face of numerous delegations coming from different backgrounds and having different perspectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is really the same spirit of mediation that the Convention itself seeks to encourage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is the first treaty named after Singapore among those concluded under the auspices of the UN, and bears testament to our extensive contributions to the development of international commercial mediation globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: On 7 August 2019, the Singapore Convention Signing Ceremony and Conference was held in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singapore hosted more than 1,500 delegates from 70 countries at the event.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The signatories included the world's two largest economies, the US and China; three of Asia's four largest economies, namely, China, India and South Korea; and five of 10 Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries, that is, Brunei, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The overwhelming response and turnout at the event were a powerful statement in support of multilateralism and a rules-based international order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, on a more specific level, the Convention is the missing third piece in the international dispute resolution enforcement framework, as many businesses today rely either on arbitration, enforced via the New York Convention, or on litigation, for cross-border disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Mediation is rising in popularity due to a growing recognition of its benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is cost-effective, flexible, efficient and also confidential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It allows parties to retain control over the outcome of their disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They control and, in fact, design the architecture of the terms on which they come and reach a settlement on their dispute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is attractive for businesses which wish to resolve their commercial disputes with an outcome that is mutually acceptable to both sides whilst preserving their long-term relationships and leaving open the possibility of working together in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The conciliatory nature of mediation reduces the instances where a dispute leads ultimately to a complete termination of commercial relationships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Mediation, therefore, complements other modes of dispute resolution, as it can be used in conjunction with litigation or arbitration, and increasingly, it often is embedded into the system and it appears in both types of dispute resolution mechanisms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A survey of participants at the 2016 Global Pound Conference found that a majority believed a greater emphasis on collaborative over adversarial process is a trend that will have the most significant influence on the future of commercial dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, with all of that, the one key challenge that has been hindering the growth and adoption of mediation is the oft-cited difficulty faced by a party in ensuring that its counter-party, that is, the party with whom it enters into a settlement agreement, complies with the terms of the agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This difficulty was also highlighted by the 2016 Global Pound Conference survey, where 51% of respondents indicated that legislation or conventions that promote the recognition and enforcement of settlements, including those reached in mediation, would most improve commercial dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There is, therefore, a need for an effective, efficient and harmonised framework to enforce cross-border commercial mediated settlement agreements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In response to this, the Convention puts in place a process for a party to enforce or invoke its settlement agreement in Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is simple to use and allows businesses to maximise the benefits of mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Businesses can have greater assurance and certainty that mediation can be relied on to settle cross-border commercial disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This, in turn, promotes investor and business confidence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Convention, therefore, facilitates the administration of international transactions by commercial parties, and we are hopeful that the establishment of a framework for the enforcement of such agreements will contribute to the development of harmonious international economic relations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Convention attained one of the highest numbers of first-day signatories for any UN trade convention, reflecting a recognition by the international community of the benefits that the Convention will bring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The signing of the Convention marks the start of a long-term commitment by Singapore to promote the Convention and its adoption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In putting together these provisions, the mechanism and also the framework, we consulted various industry stakeholders, including international dispute resolution institutions and experts, and received their feedback, both in terms of the philosophy behind the enforcement and also the practical aspects of enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill is intended to operate in parallel with the Mediation Act 2017.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: That is the Act which Members will be familiar with, that deals with enforcement of mediated agreements domestically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It also preserves contractual remedies, with a view to giving commercial parties a broad suite of choices to enforce or choose to invoke their international mediated settlement agreements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The key features of the Bill include the following.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill relates to the cross-border enforcement of mediated settlement agreements and the invocation of such agreements as a defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In other words, if a party chooses to act and bring a claim in breach of a prior mediated settlement agreement to which the claim applies, then the agreement can also be invoked as a defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It covers international settlement agreements resulting from mediation concluded by parties to resolve a commercial dispute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Agreements that are excluded from the Bill are those that (a) have been approved by a court or concluded in the course of court proceedings and are enforceable as judgments; (b) are enforceable as arbitral awards; and (c) relate to certain subject matters, such as family, inheritance and employment law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As mentioned, the Bill provides a range of options for parties seeking to enforce or invoke their settlement agreements in Singapore under the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These are set out in clause 4 of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With these options, parties have the flexibility to decide on the most appropriate mode for their own particular situation and circumstance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will help them to assess the options better and also save time and costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill provides a "Court order mechanism" for parties seeking to enforce or invoke their settlement agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, a party can apply to the High Court to record its settlement agreement as an order of Court, which can thereafter be used for the purposes of enforcement, or as I mentioned earlier, as a defence, as the case may be.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The procedure and the framework are similar to the enforcement of awards under the International Arbitration Act, which the legal and business communities would already be familiar with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It also provides greater certainty if future reliance on the settlement agreement is necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For the avoidance of doubt, the process of obtaining a Court order under the Bill does not extinguish the underlying mediated settlement agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It preserves the status of the underlying mediated agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, it is still an agreement after all, even if one chooses to invoke the Court process for the purposes of enforcement or to raise it as a defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Either party to the mediated settlement agreement is at liberty to use the underlying settlement agreement for enforcement or invocation in another country, which is a party to the Convention, which is precisely why there is such a Convention – for cross-border enforcement of the mediated settlement agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This, of course, will be subject to that country's own procedures for enforcement and/or invocation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, where there are existing proceedings in the High Court or the Court of Appeal, a party can apply to Court to invoke the settlement agreement as a defence, to prove that the matter in those proceedings had already been resolved by the settlement agreement, without the need to take out separate proceedings to rely on the agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This also helps save time and costs for parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Lastly, parties’ legal rights and remedies existing outside of the Convention will be preserved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This means that parties can, for instance, continue to rely on contractual principles to enforce or invoke their settlement agreement, should they prefer this route.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, clause 6 requires the applicant to provide certain documents and evidence to the Court with its application.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Court may also take into account an exhaustive list of grounds to refuse an application under clause 7.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where a settlement agreement has been recorded as an order of Court, clause 8 enables a party to apply to set aside the Court order under stipulated grounds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: That is a choice given to the parties; you might decide that you wish to opt out of the modalities set out in the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The related amendments to the Mediation Act 2017 provide that a settlement agreement within the scope of the Bill is not precluded from the Mediation Act 2017, if that settlement agreement also qualifies under that Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In other words, it preserves a party's rights to go under the Mediation Act 2017 if you also qualify under the framework of that legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments to SCJA provide the High Court with the jurisdiction to grant applications under the Bill.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It represents a significant major step for cross-border resolution of commercial disputes.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is with the hope that businesses will benefit with more certainty and assurance.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Mediation is now getting more popular and thus more frequently used at both domestic and international platforms.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify if the service will be provided by a list of approved vendors globally or the parties involved will have to source for this themselves?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Next, can the Senior Minister of State please outline if the Courts of signatory countries will handle applications to enforce or clear parties involved?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Some major nations have not ratified the Convention.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are there specific reasons or considerations for this?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With a Bill as this under the umbrella of the UN, it would be excellent to have as many nations come on board and, if not so, the reasons, perhaps could be addressed adequately.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I believe there are also some inconsistencies with the fundamentals of commercial mediation in the Western jurisdiction.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps the Senior Minister of State is probably more well-versed with this, and if it is possible, perhaps he can enlighten us on some of the possible reasons for this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The mediation industry is variable across different countries and jurisdictions.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For example, in the UK, it has a well-known reputation and history of being strong in arbitration.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What is important in considering this Bill is the fact that mediation will be driven very much by the local framework, culture and emphasis.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Mediator recognition, training and qualifications also vary across the globe.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Cultural diversity will exist and we know that "culture can, indeed, trump strategy".

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In view of all these factors, how do we ensure some degree of consistency and standardisation?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Another concern is on the requirement of having "the mediator signing the document".

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: A mediator's document is quite different from a witness' statement in Court, for example.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In some places, the mediator may not be comfortable to have his or her name and documents appear and be utilised in a Court of law.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Mediators may disagree to sign the Settlement Agreement and, if they are not comfortable with this, to be also subpoenaed as witnesses.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Some cases or disputes put up for mediation may span a period of time, maybe even years, and agreement may not have been reached at the first sitting.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If an agreement is then eventually reached, how can we prove that it is actually settled through mediation and not due to other platforms, alternatives and various permutations of interventions, during the course of the matter in question?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And what if both parties are at loggerheads pertaining to this?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, these are some of the clarifications I have.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I rise in support of this Bill, which seeks to enhance the dispute resolution landscape within Singapore, by giving greater recognition towards mediation and international commercial settlement agreements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, mediation accords parties greater control over the outcome and resolution of the matter, which contrasts with long-drawn Court trials, where the outcome of a case rests in the Judge’s hands.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, the contents of parties' disputes are kept confidential, unlike litigation where parties' dirty linen and affairs are often aired in Court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, legal costs are reduced, as parties no longer have to pay for their lawyers' fees and Court fees once a settlement has been reached.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Lastly and most importantly, parties' relationships are preserved and this is essential where parties wish to continue business relations with each other.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As Singapore recognises the benefits of mediation and continues to develop its position as a leading global dispute resolution hub, mediation institutions and schemes will take on an increasingly important role.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Many individuals have saved time and costs and would likewise recommend SMC to others involved in disputes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Apart from SMC, we also have the International Institute of Mediators (Singapore) Limited (iiM), which was established as a result of its founding members’ commitment to develop and promote the mediation profession on a global basis.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Aside from the regular mediation sessions conducted by its members, the iiM additionally provides education and training for those who aspire to become trained mediators.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am also pleased to share that the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC’s) Freelancers and Self-Employed Unit (UFSE) and iiM have inked a collaboration agreement in December 2019 to better serve the needs of the freelancer community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is one of the many initiatives illustrating the Labour Movement's commitment towards its freelancer members, ensuring that they have an appropriate avenue for amicable dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With this collaboration, NTUC UFSE members will be able to enjoy discounted rates for mediation services provided by iiM.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Turning now to the international commercial sphere, with the increasing prevalence of global and international trade between countries, coupled with Singapore’s open and highly developed free-market economy, the need for cross-border mediation resources and enforceable international settlement agreements becomes particularly crucial.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is against this commercial backdrop that this Bill is commendable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By the same token, the settlement agreement may also be invoked by a party as a defence against a claim that has already been settled.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This prevents settled disputes from being re-litigated, which saves parties’ time and costs as well as judicial resources.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the Bill is no doubt commendable, I have the following questions and clarifications for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Bill only applies to international commercial settlement agreements resulting from mediation and does not extend to settlement agreements concluded for family, inheritance and/or employment disputes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, is there a reason why the Bill is not extended to these other areas of dispute?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If so, would the Minister be willing to share the reasons?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Also, does the Minister foresee that there should be a similar Bill covering these other areas, given today's globally interconnected world, where many individuals opt to work around the globe, having assets typically situated in different parts of the world and where transactions cut across borders?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, given the growing freelancer community and, especially for those who look to venture overseas, whether digitally or in person, would the Bill also cover intellectual property (IP) rights?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, I understand that the Court retains the discretion to refuse the application to record the agreement as a Court Order if there was a serious breach by the mediator of the applicable standards.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What are some examples of serious breaches by the mediator which would warrant the Court’s refusal of the application?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: And is it necessary to refuse enforcement, especially if commercial entities have been properly advised and have the freedom to enter into such settlement agreements?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, we do see a greater trend towards mediation over the years, especially with the implementation of the Mediation Act in 2017 and the various mediation institutions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have also seen some choosing mediation over litigation, while others opt to use mediation in conjunction with litigation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would the Minister foresee a further increase in disputes resolved as a result of the new Bill and, if so, to what extent?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would the Minister also be able to share some of the views and concerns of the legal fraternity as well as the business community, in response to this new Bill?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As a representative of the business community, I strongly believe in the benefits of mediation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I constantly advocate mediation as the initial avenue for dispute resolution as the flexibility and advantages that mediation offers are wide-ranging.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The benefits of mediation vis-à-vis arbitration and litigation are frequently cited to be time and cost efficiency, confidentiality, non-confrontational character and, many times, the business relationship may continue after a mediation settlement is reached.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I believe I can say that, lawyers apart, one of the most stressful things in life for the everyday man on the street would be to be hit with legal matters, especially a full-blown litigious trial.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The stress, worry and uncertainty are exacerbated by a largely adversarial process that takes much time and, indeed, resources away from the real business of doing business.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the business community will benefit if mediation becomes a widely-accepted and recognised avenue for dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With mediation, the options for settlement are wider in scope than the monetary compensation available through arbitration or litigation and parties have a chance to negotiate settlement options without prejudice to their legal rights and in a non-pressure cooker atmosphere.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The confidential nature of mediation also protects companies from unwanted public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Most business relationships are complex and forged over time and, as such, I believe most would seek to preserve the relationship where possible.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As the awareness for mediation grows, I see this as a cost- and time-efficient option for companies to resolve disputes.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As the President of SMF, I have personally facilitated dialogue between SMC and SMF.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The hope of both parties is to bring greater awareness of the options and advantages of mediation to the manufacturing community and thus fostering greater acceptance of this avenue of dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is really amazing, as compared to the significantly longer processes of arbitration and litigation with the corresponding higher professional service fees that one would have to pay.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is my hope that more trade associations and chambers will take the lead in spreading what mediation is and help our society to be one that is less litigious.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is in this context that I firmly place my support behind this Bill.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the main reason why companies hesitate to consider mediation as an avenue of dispute resolution was the lack of an enforcement mechanism, especially in the event of cross-border interests.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As there was a lack of a cross-border framework for mediated settlement agreements, parties are only able to seek enforcement of the settlement agreement under contract law.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: By passing this Bill as a step towards ratifying the Singapore Convention, mediation will now be further seen as one that does not waste time and one that can produce desired outcomes.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With a global framework in place, businesses should have greater confidence to settle international disputes through mediation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong at the signing ceremony, "This will help advance international trade, commerce and investment." The ratifying of the Convention in the near future will be a step forward for the international business community as signatory states move to standardise enforcement of mediation settlements in their respective jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Once again, businesses will not see benefits overnight as legislation takes time to be enacted.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, we hope to be able to lay the groundwork and build awareness in the immediate future.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is timely, especially with the recent coming into force of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and the European Union–Singapore Free Trade Agreement (EUSFTA).

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As a trade federation, SMF has increasingly encouraged our local companies to look beyond our shores and seek out business partners in new markets for growth.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The top three destinations in the survey were Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In 2019, SMF welcomed 21 international business delegations and hosted eight business matching sessions for the local and international business representatives.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The Enterprise Europe Network (EEN) Singapore Chapter is managed by SMF and, in the lead up to the ratification of the EUSFTA, saw an increase in interest from local business owners during the visits and business-matching sessions for the European delegations.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, finding a viable business partner does not happen over one business-matching session.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The process usually requires a long period of discussion and gestation before an agreement is finalised.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Forging business relationships in new markets is a challenging endeavour, especially in markets with very different cultures and regulatory requirements.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With increased cross-border commercial transactions, it is expected that differences will arise.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As such, a mediation framework that is internationally recognised is much needed for a fair and efficient way to resolve disputes in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, the business community is fortunate to operate in a stable environment built on the trust and respect of the Government, employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Mediation actually embodies the key tenets of open communication and trust that lie in the foundation of our Tripartite Partnership.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: My hope is for mediation to continue to be seen as a viable first approach to not only resolve employer and employee disputes but as an avenue to resolve business disputes as well.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill is important for Singapore’s ratification of the Convention.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Among the signatories were the United States, China, India and South Korea.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is needed is for states to align international processes with its international obligation and then ratify the Convention.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My questions are: is the Ministry aware of other states’ progress in this process?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And how has Singapore been engaging other countries in encouraging them to ratify?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Convention plays a key role in Singapore's future in the international sphere.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not only is this Convention the first UN treaty named after Singapore, but it is also in line with Singapore’s role as an international dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As an international dispute resolution hub, Singapore has many dispute resolution tools available.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me at this stage, Sir, to declare that I am a practising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has a strong presence in arbitration and also offers a special judicial process through the Singapore International Commercial Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is also a party to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements and the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These conventions provide for foreign recognition and enforcement of Singapore Court orders and arbitration awards made in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through this, Singapore is better positioned to be a dispute resolution hub as parties are able to resolve their disputes either through the Court, through arbitration or even voluntarily through mediation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 4 allows for such an application by a party to the settlement agreement, and clause 5 provides that the High Court may grant such leave to record the order as an order of Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order for parties to utilise this regime, clause 6 sets out that the two following documents and evidence are necessary: one, the international settlement agreement signed by the parties; and two, evidence that the international settlement agreement resulted from mediation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second criterion is important as it helps distinguish between a contractual agreement and a mediation settlement.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although both are formed only when parties consent voluntarily to something, a mediation settlement requires there to have been a dispute and may even be directly enforced as a Court order and not merely a contractual agreement.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If this distinction were to be blurred, the special statutory regime that elevates private agreements to Court orders may be abused.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is required is the mediator's signature on the international settlement agreement, a document signed by the mediator indicating that mediation was carried out and an attestation by the institution that administered the mediation or any other evidence acceptable to the Court per clause 6(1)(b).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unlike the Mediation Act 2017, which allows for the mediation to be carried out either by a designated mediation service provider or conducted by a certified mediator in section 12(3)(a), clause 6(b)(iii) of the Bill requires that the mediation be administered by an institution and not merely a certified mediator.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, my question for the Senior Minister of State is: would the Senior Minister of State kindly elaborate on how institutions for mediation in Singapore are building up their capacity and capabilities in preparation for the commencement of the Singapore Convention?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides the formal requirements for the application listed in clause 6, clause 7 sets out substantive grounds for refusing an application to record an international settlement agreement as an order of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 7(2)(c)(i) provides that evidence that the obligations in the international settlement agreement have been performed can be a ground for refusing an application to record it as a Court order.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because an application to record an order may be to prove that the matter has already been resolved and not just for enforcement of the agreement, it is good that ultimately it is up to the Court’s discretion whether to refuse the application notwithstanding there is such evidence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 7(2)(d) retains flexibility for parties to agree to opt out of this statutory enforcement regime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the event that they do not wish to allow their international settlement agreement to be recorded before the Court, there still is flexibility to do so.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 8 is interesting in that it addresses a situation where an already mediated international settlement agreement is recorded as an order of Court but the other party to the settlement agreement does not appear before the Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Court proceedings are mandatory in the sense that they force the other party to participate and appear in Court, otherwise a judgment may be entered against them, for example, a judgment in default of appearance situations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the other hand, voluntariness of both parties to a certain extent is necessary in order to resolve the dispute via mediation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Following the commencement of the Convention, the jurisprudence and scholarship relating to mediation will probably continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State elaborate on what the Ministry is doing to encourage and equip Singapore lawyers to be active and effective members in the mediation industry as well as to develop strong thought leadership in this area – whether in the academics, whether as a practitioner or whether as a mediator – him or herself?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State kindly clarify that, please?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as it is anticipated that the use of mediation as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism will pick up around the world following commencement and ratification of the Singapore Convention, it is commendable that law students are also looking to further their interests and passions in this area already.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, Singapore held its first-ever international moot for university students that focuses on mediation advocacy and mediation proper.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I ask the Senior Minister of State: would the Senior Minister of State share with us what efforts are being done to sustain interest in development in this area of mediation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mediation has been growing in prominence in Singapore's dispute resolution landscape.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One starting point for institutionalised mediation in Singapore could be then Attorney-General Chan Sek Keong's speech at the Opening of the Legal Year 1996 on the need to look into mediation as a form of alternative dispute resolution and the suggestion to establish a commercial mediation centre.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Since then, Singapore has made great leaps in institutionalised mediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2020, we now have a proliferation of mediation institutes, including the Singapore Mediation Centre (SMC), the Singapore International Mediation Centre (SIMC), and the Singapore International Mediation Institute (SIMI), among others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Presumption of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) applies for all civil cases under the State Courts Practice Directions, which requires cases to be referred to the most appropriate mode of ADR, including mediation, as a first resort.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Amongst the significant developments introduced by this Act was allowing mediated settlement agreements to be recorded and enforced as Court judgments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is thus a point of much pride that the progress Singapore has made on mediation domestically is now magnified on the international stage through the Singapore Convention on Mediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similar to the Singapore Mediation Act, it addresses the non-enforceability of mediated settlement agreements, which has been traditionally an obstacle to the adoption of mediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The 1958 New York convention, which streamlined the enforcement of foreign arbitral awards led to the boom in arbitration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is hoped that the Singapore Convention on Mediation will now put international mediation on an even footing as international arbitration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is currently no single set of mediation standards in Singapore or internationally.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: SMC has a Code of Conduct for its mediators in sessions held by SMC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: SIMI has a Code of Professional Conduct applicable to any mediation that is mediated by an SIMI Mediator, while the Society of Mediation Professionals (Singapore) is a group of mediators looking to develop a collective, localised and contextualised code of ethics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is in relation to section 7(2)(e), which states that only a "serious breach" by the mediator justifies the Court refusing to grant relief.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Convention and the Bill do not define what constitutes a "serious breach".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A further hurdle, again, to determining what is a "serious breach" is the fragmented state of mediation standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third clarification is on civil justice reforms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Convention and the Bill enable the enforcement of mediated international settlement agreements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Domestically, the enforcement process for civil judgments is under review.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Civil Justice Review Committee's (CJRC's) report noted that the "tools currently available for enforcing both monetary and non-monetary judgments are limited and unsophisticated".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It further noted that the enforcement process is too Court-centric and that there are limited modes of enforcing non-monetary judgments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CJRC recommended that the enforcement process for civil judgments be privatised and that the Ministry study the problems and proposals further.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also suggested that the Ministry implement civil enforcement reforms separately from the rest of the civil justice reforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the progress of ratification of the Convention by other states and when the Convention will come into effect.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: He also asked how Singapore has been engaging other countries in encouraging them to join us in seeking to first sign up to, and subsequently, ratify the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore hopes to be amongst the first countries to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The overwhelming show of support for the Convention on the day it opened for signature is itself encouraging, and this suggests many other countries share our view that mediation is increasingly prevalent and overall helpful to the conduct of international business transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This gives us a good basis to believe that the other states will also quickly ratify the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We understand several other countries are taking active steps towards their own ratification process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Like us, they will have to go through their own internal process and approvals, such as enacting domestic legislation to implement the obligations contained in the Convention, before they subsequently ratify the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On our end, what we have done is we have offered to host workshops for those other countries interested in finding out about the Convention, what it takes to have that implemented in their own domestic laws and also to be able to assist where required in their ratification processes as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, a series of other related events, conferences, sessions, including the competition that Mr Christopher de Souza spoke about earlier will take place in September 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will also include workshops for interested government officials, legal and business communities, academics and, of course, students from around the world, and this will provide participants with an insight into the Convention and sharing information and thought leadership on the latest developments in not just mediation but also the broader realm of dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are overall hopeful that the Convention will come into force soon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked if we foresee an increase in disputes resolved as a result of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Well, that is certainly the intention behind the Bill and the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Several Members have already touched on these benefits, which include time and cost efficiency, greater party autonomy and control over the resolution of the disputes, how they frame disputes, how they frame the settlement of the disputes and the terms and conditions which go behind such agreements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mediation also protects confidentiality between the parties and, ultimately, also preserves a relationship which may have taken years, if not decades, to build.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that is the overarching benefit in engaging mediation as a method of resolving disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I would agree with Members that these factors add to the reasons why we believe that mediation is growing as one of the key dispute resolution options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Douglas Foo made an important point when he spoke about the importance of educating the business community of the benefits of mediation and of how these reforms can impact them positively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I agree, and the efforts to raise awareness of the Convention and of mediation in particular, must be an ongoing and long-term one, and we are committed to doing so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw and our Singapore mediation institutes which many Members have mentioned – the SIMC, SIMI which is the mediation institute – have taken active steps in the community to raise awareness of the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw has been actively promoting the Convention and its benefits to the legal and business communities and to schools through conferences, seminars, workshops and other outreach efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIMC has been conducting briefing sessions in conjunction with organisations, such as the Law Society and Singapore Corporate Counsel Association, to reach out to the legal profession and to the industry players and they will continue to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Thus far, SIMI – the institute – has conducted "Mediation In Practice" seminars for professionals in the healthcare and built environment sectors – two sectors which we believe will benefit from the usage of mediation – and will continue to conduct seminars for other sectors as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also specifically asked about MinLaw’s efforts to build capability, interest and thought leadership with regard to mediation generally amongst mediation institutions, amongst Singapore lawyers and law students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But before I do so, I think Mr Christopher de Souza noted that clause 6(1)(b)(iii) requires that the mediation be administered by an institution and not merely by a certified mediator.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I would just like to add that the requirements in 6(1)(b) are disjunctive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Alternatively, the mediator’s signature on the agreement or some other document, not necessarily on the mediated agreement or any other evidence acceptable to the Court, will also suffice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, clause 6(1)(b) provides for a broad spectrum of different options by which the Court might then gain insight as to whether there is evidence supporting the contention that this agreement has arisen from mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore’s mediation institutions have built a strong pool of qualified mediators and practitioners and this started even before the Convention was inked last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIMC and SMC, which are two of the designated mediation service providers under the Mediation Act 2017, have established panels of mediators with broad expertise in very diverse fields.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They have expertise in different fields as well, different subject matters, which are important because, whilst a dispute might centre around the law, the subject matter of the dispute might well come from different spectrums of society and different aspects of business transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Knowledge, know-how and thought leadership are important drivers for mediation as a practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And to this end, our institutions regularly conduct courses to equip Singapore lawyers and other professionals as well with mediation knowledge and skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They include senior counsel, managing partners and partners of law firms in Singapore, general counsel of multinational corporations located in Singapore and also other large companies, and SIMC subsequently appointed them as specialist mediators in January this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIMC will be looking to conduct more runs of such specialist training workshops for lawyers, inhouse counsel and other business professionals, the thinking behind that being that it is not just within the province and domain of lawyers to conduct and run mediations but rather that if we bring the skill inhouse into the business environment, then it is more likely that mediation will be taken up as an option, and also, would be able to locate such expertise within the business itself to catch hold of the dispute as early as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On thought leadership, the Singapore International Dispute Resolution Academy (SIDRA) was established as a platform for thought leadership in dispute resolution theory, practice and policy, and this includes, of course, the area of mediation as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIDRA strengthens Singapore’s thought leadership in this area through its research projects, such as its Singapore Convention on Mediation research project, which produced the first commentary on the Convention, and the International Dispute Resolution Survey research project, which captured respondents’ considerations in the use of international commercial dispute resolution, including arbitration, mediation and litigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On law students, which Mr Christopher de Souza mentioned, we have not forgotten them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I think Mr Christopher de Souza mentioned that SIMI organised the inaugural International Mediation Singapore moot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That involved 140 students from 30 different universities from around the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It was the first international moot organised in Singapore that focuses on mediation advocacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This year, in conjunction with what I mentioned earlier on the “Singapore Convention Week” in September this year, we will also have the second instalment of this programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To further develop students’ interest in mediation, NUS, SMU and SUSS law students are provided with electives and modules on mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIMI supported the founding of, and continues to advise, the NUS Collaborative Dispute Resolution (CDR) Club, a dedicated club for law students to organise activities related to CDR, such as selections for international competitions, events, seminars and also hosting actual competitions for students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This month, they will be organising a Mediation Advocacy Competition for contestants to pit their advocacy skills to further their client's interests in collaborative mediation settings – real-life settings but students have a chance to apply what they have been taught and put into practice in as realistic a setting as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIMI and SIMC also provide internships for students interested in deepening their own understanding of mediation and how it applies in practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked about the views and concerns of the legal fraternity and the business community in response to the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In some ways, the response from the legal community to what I have outlined over the last couple of minutes, from attending the Convention to the training, to coming forward to serve as specialist mediators, they all tell us that the legal community and the businesses one sees value in mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw also conducted several engagement sessions with professional bodies, business associations and students, and received very positive feedback for which we are very heartened.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the international front, the adoption of the Convention by the UN General Assembly, Singapore's signing of the Convention and the other countries indicating that they would wish to ratify the Convention as soon as they can, they all bode well and they give us good reason to be quietly optimistic that the Convention will be ratified by more countries, and also its application to businesses across different jurisdictions to promote international trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef asked if an agreement arising from mediation will now be enforceable under the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Louis Ng noted quite rightly that as part of the civil justice reforms, the enforcement process of civil judgments in Singapore is currently under review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: He asked how this review will affect the processes under this Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under the Bill, an application for recognition of the international settlement agreement has to be applied for through the Court process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I have outlined that earlier when I made the speech yesterday.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One of the objectives of the civil justice reforms is to enhance the efficiency of the Court procedures and this would also help the process under this Bill because the processes will be streamlined, enhanced and made more efficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef had asked whether an international settlement agreement resulting from mediation can be enforced under the Convention regardless of its place of origin, and whether a party seeking to enforce such an agreement can do so in the state where the other party has a majority of its assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a classic enforcement issue that almost all lawyers face when they look at how to or where to enforce an award or order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Obviously so, because it can be enforced only against the party in a Convention jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This provides businesses and investors with the certainty upfront that their cross-border transactions, which subsequently result in a dispute, which can then be mediated, can be easily and, in my view, more effectively enforced, if one is able to discern how and where to go, depending on the assets located of the counter party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A party is also not limited to seeking enforcement under the Convention in just one jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I explained in my speech yesterday, obtaining an order of Court under this Bill for the purposes of the enforcement does not extinguish the underlying mediated agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Either party to the mediated settlement agreement is at liberty to continue using the settlement agreement for enforcement or invocation in another jurisdiction which is a party to the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, you can go and seek enforcement of the mediated agreement in different jurisdictions, but provided that these different jurisdictions are Convention jurisdictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is also subject, as in all cases, to the jurisdiction's own domestic procedures for enforcement and invocation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, other countries will have their own process as we have set out in this Bill, and compliance with that process must be adhered to, which is not uncommon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Article 1(3)(a) of the Convention excludes settlements that have been approved by the Court or concluded in the course of proceedings before a Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, sometimes, in the course of Court proceedings, you have a settlement agreement that arises in the context of that, this Bill does not apply to those agreements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, however, does not mean that when a settlement agreement has been recorded as a Court order under the Bill, for the purposes of enforcement or invocation in Singapore, that parties to the agreement would thereafter be precluded from presenting the same agreement in another jurisdiction for enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, I just want to make this clear, that in coming to Court in Singapore, adhering to the process under this Bill, for the purposes of enforcing or invoking the settlement agreement, does not preclude you from taking this agreement to another jurisdiction and then complying with the domestic procedures and laws, and also then enforcing it in that jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for the reasons behind the Bill being limited to commercial matters and why the Bill does not extend to agreements concluded for family, inheritance or employment disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The rationale of that is because it is consistent with the UN Commission on International Trade Law's (UNCITRAL's) mandate to focus on commercial disputes and commercial matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, in its deliberations on the draft Convention text, commercial disputes were the main focus of the Working Group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Working Group decided that settlement agreements dealing with family and labour law matters and other areas where party autonomy might be limited due to overriding mandatory rules or public policy, should be excluded from the scope of the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Further, in matters, such as family and employment law, domestic laws and public policy considerations often differ from one country to another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This could become an issue if a foreign court is faced with an application for the enforcement or invocation of agreements that might otherwise be contrary to its own laws and public policy of that particular jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That said, Mr Patrick Tay might wish to know that family disputes and related international mediated agreements are currently being considered by the Hague Conference on Private International Law, on whether there is scope for an international instrument to be developed for such matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, that might well happen, but perhaps within a differentiated set of rules, given the public policy considerations I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked if the Bill will cover intellectual property (IP) rights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Working Group agreed not to define the term "commercial" but left it to interpretation and further agreed that it should be capable of being given a wide interpretation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Often, one finds that a dispute can raise multifaceted issues, it is not often easy to pigeonhole into one category or another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, so long as the settlement agreement pertaining to or touching on IP rights relates to matters arising from a commercial dispute, then it can fall within the scope of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef asked if the courts of signatory countries will handle the applications for the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Convention provides for a competent authority designated by a party to handle and hear applications brought under the Convention in that country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is not limited to the courts of a country, and other bodies deemed suitable and competent by that country could also be designated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef asked how parties can prove that the settlement agreement was a result of mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I believe Mr Christopher de Souza also raised this point earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is not uncommon for parties to discuss and come to a resolution through various channels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, in other words, where there is a dispute, one does not just sit down and say, "Okay, listen, this is a mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Often, there is a series of informal discussions, maybe exchange in writing sometimes or over meetings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can happen for a period of time before arriving at an agreement through the mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where the dispute is eventually resolved through these steps and recorded in the form of an agreement at a mediation session, the Bill will be applicable, subject to the other conditions of the Bill being met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, such evidence can be in the form of a document signed by the mediator conducting the mediation indicating that such a mediation was carried out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On this note, Prof Fatimah Lateef raised the concern about the mediator having to sign the settlement agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In line with Article 4(1) of the Convention, the requirements set out in clause 6(1)(b) are not exhaustive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The first option for demonstrating that the agreement resulted from mediation is, of course, the mediator’s signature on the mediated agreement itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This might be the simplest and neatest method of satisfying the requirement, although in some jurisdictions, including in Singapore, it is not the practice to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is not the practice to include the mediator as a party to the agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, on occasion, if the parties subsequently disagree on the terms, it should not be open to the parties to call the mediator as a witness to come and give a testimony as to what actually transpired.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, for that reason, mediators generally do not sign off on the mediated agreement itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But as Prof Fatimah Lateef correctly points out, there are other options that this Bill has made available, other mechanisms by which this can be done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One option is that separate document that I mentioned earlier, signed by the mediator who conducted it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If none of these available options can be used to prove, then parties can rely on clause 6(1)(b)(iv), which states that "any other evidence" acceptable to the authority before which the application is made can be used.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, it might well be a combination of emails, something in writing, something verbal, which goes towards proving that the mediation took place and that this agreement arose as a result of those discussions and negotiations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the requirement for a certified English translation of a settlement agreement drafted in a foreign language to be provided to the Court, Prof Fatimah Lateef asked whether the Bill will provide for a list of approved translators globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Consistent with the usual practice of proceedings in our Courts, parties are free to engage their own qualified translators for the translation for the purposes of clause 6(4) of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Neither the Convention nor the Bill stipulates a list of approved global translators nor is there a requirement to provide such a list.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if the intention is for the industry to self-regulate or if MinLaw intends to consolidate a single set of standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Louis Ng also asked about the definition of serious breaches and what might warrant the Court's refusal of an application under the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef noted that local frameworks and culture may drive the conduct of mediation differently in each country, which is a fair point, and queried whether and how the Bill will ensure consistency and standards for mediators before whom agreements are concluded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, as noted by Prof Fatimah Lateef herself, given the varying nature of mediation and the forms it can take across different countries, languages, cultures, it would itself be a challenge to now prescribe common standards applicable across different countries which signed up to the Convention as being the applicable standards for mediation in all cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, the UN Working Group, when looking at the issue, considered an illustrative list of examples of potentially applicable mediator standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But these are standards that we would not be surprised to see in any application to enforce an arbitral award or a Court order, or indeed, a mediated settlement agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, these are issues, such as the independence of the mediator, the impartiality, confidentiality and whether or not there has been natural justice and fair treatment of the parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are all standards that you find in one form or another replicated in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, the Working Group also noted that standards and applicable standards might change, might shift.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There might be more or less emphasis on one point or another subsequently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, I would also note that the mediation landscape in Singapore is still developing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, Mr Louis Ng is right in noting that mediation institutions like SMC and SIMC already require mediators on their panels to adhere to a code of conduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also have SIMI, the accreditation body for mediation in Singapore, which sets standards for mediator training and also accreditation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If the mediators are from certain professions, such as the legal profession or the accounting profession, they will also be subject to their professions' own set of standards on ethical rules and other professional guidelines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I am sure Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Patrick Tay would know, the Courts would apply those standards, looking at it in the context of what it means by drawing parallels with arbitrator misconduct, for instance, or the rules of how a fair arbitration might have taken place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Those principles, whilst not directly relevant to a mediation in the same way, would no doubt guide the conduct of the Courts as to what comprises "serious breach".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is to ensure that mediator and mediation standards continue to be upheld and are not undermined in the process of concluding a settlement agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore continues to position itself as a thought leader, as a hub, as I mentioned at the outset, for all forms of dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And with the Convention and this Bill, we will expect to see that the third of the more popular areas of dispute resolution will now have an avenue for cross-border enforcement, that, in our view, will promote international trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With the milestone that we have achieved with the Convention, Mr Deputy Speaker, we believe that this Bill will bring rich and varied opportunities to our businesses, mediation institutions and professionals and also our legal profession.
